text: Every Snort and Suricata rule follows the same basic shape once you know what to look for. This lesson walks through that shape piece by piece, then applies it to one real, simplified rule so the syntax stops looking like noise.

A rule starts with an action — alert, drop, pass, or reject — telling the engine exactly what to do when traffic matches. Next comes the protocol, like tcp, udp, or icmp, followed by the source IP and port, a direction operator, and the destination IP and port, which together describe exactly which traffic the rule applies to. Everything after that, inside the parentheses, is a set of rule options that describe precisely what to look for in that traffic and how to describe the match once it fires.

Take a real, simplified example: alert tcp any any -> $HOME_NET 80, followed by options in parentheses. Alert means it only raises an alert, not a block. tcp any any means any TCP traffic from any source and port. The arrow points toward $HOME_NET port 80 — our own web servers. Together, that line says: watch for any TCP traffic headed to our web servers on port 80.

Inside the parentheses, msg gives the human-readable description that shows up in the alert, something like 'Possible SQL Injection Attempt' — the first thing an analyst reads. content specifies the exact byte pattern to search for inside the packet's payload; here, the literal string UNION SELECT, a telltale sign of a SQL injection attempt. sid is a unique numeric ID that every custom rule must have, so an analyst or another tool can reference that exact rule later without ambiguity, and rev tracks which revision of the rule is currently running, which matters once a rule gets tuned more than once.
With the syntax down, next we'll compare two deployment models for IDS itself: network-based IDS watching traffic on the wire, versus host-based IDS watching a single system from the inside.
